claims.text: Uniformly dispersed Cr-rich nano-precipitates in low-alloy steels promote formation of a stable, compact passive oxide film.
Cr-rich nano-precipitates interrupt continuous corrosion pathways.
The precipitate-induced passive film reduces localized corrosion attack.
The proposed precipitate structure enhances corrosion resistance in both nuclear-power and chemical-processing environments.
A quench-and-temper treatment followed by an isothermal hold near 500°C for several hours will induce a fine, uniform dispersion of Cr-rich nano-precipitates in low-alloy steel.
The concentration and morphology of Cr-rich precipitates are sensitive to thermal exposure conditions.
The Cr-rich nano-precipitates act as nucleation sites for passive oxide formation.
The Cr-rich nano-precipitates disrupt pathways used by aggressive corrosive agents.
The nano-precipitates act as local physical barriers to corrosion propagation.
The nano-precipitates promote homogeneous nucleation and growth of a compact, chemically stable passive film.
The modified passive film resists breakdown by altering local electrochemical kinetics.
A compact passive oxide film can exhibit high impedance and capacitive behavior in EIS measurements.
Treated samples will have lower corrosion current densities than conventionally processed controls.
Treated samples will have higher passive-film breakdown potentials than conventionally processed controls.
Treated samples will form more uniform and stable passive films than conventionally processed controls.
Precipitate coarsening outside the optimized heat-treatment window may diminish the corrosion-resistance benefit.
The study will compare treated and conventionally processed low-alloy-steel samples under otherwise identical electrochemical test conditions in two corrosive environments.
Corrosion current, breakdown potential, EIS response, passive-film morphology, and precipitate stability are measurable indicators of the proposed effect.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant corrosion-resistance improvement or a correlation between precipitates and improved passive-film characteristics would falsify the hypothesis.
